title: Central Limit Theorem
body:
**The most important theorem in the subject**, and the reason the rest of [[STATISTICS]] is
possible at all.

> Take independent samples of size $n$ from *any* population with mean $\mu$ and finite standard
> deviation $\sigma$. As $n$ grows, the [[Sampling Distribution|sampling distribution]] of
> $\bar{X}$ approaches
> $$
> \bar{X} \sim N\!\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)
> $$

The centre and the spread were already known from [[Sampling Distribution]]. **What the CLT adds is
the shape, and it adds it for free.** The population can be skewed, bimodal, discrete, uniform, or
something nobody has a name for, and the distribution of its sample means still goes normal.

## Why that is worth so much

Because it means you never need to know the population's distribution. Without the CLT, inference
about a mean would require identifying the population's exact family first, which is usually
impossible. With it, one procedure works everywhere:

- every $z$- and $t$-interval in [[Confidence Interval]]
- every test statistic in [[Hypothesis Testing]], all of which have the form
  $(\text{estimate} - \text{claim})/\text{standard error}$ and are compared against a normal or $t$
  curve
- the inference on slopes in [[Linear Regression]]

None of those care what the raw data looked like. **That is the CLT being spent.**

It also explains why the [[Normal Distribution]] turns up in nature so often: any quantity that is
a sum of many small independent contributions inherits the shape by this theorem, whether or not
the contributions are bell shaped themselves.

## The conditions, which do matter

| Condition | What breaks without it |
|---|---|
| Independent observations | everything; correlated data has a smaller effective $n$ |
| Finite $\sigma$ | heavy-tailed populations (Cauchy) never converge |
| $n$ large enough | the approximation is just bad |

"Large enough" is **$n \geq 30$** as the standard rule of thumb, but the honest version is that it
depends on the skew. A symmetric population is fine at $n = 5$; a badly skewed one may need
hundreds. For a proportion the usual check is $np \geq 10$ and $n(1-p) \geq 10$, which is the
binomial version of the same demand.

**Note what it does not say.** The *data* does not become normal, ever. Sampling more from a skewed
population gives you more skewed data. Only the distribution of the **mean** goes normal, and
mixing those two claims up is the standard misreading.

## Related

- [[Sampling Distribution]]: the centre and standard error this completes
- [[Normal Distribution]]: the limit it converges to
- [[Confidence Interval]] and [[Hypothesis Testing]]: what it is spent on
- [[Variance]]: $\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \sigma^2/n$, the spread half of the statement
- [[Simulation]] and [[Random Numbers]] ([[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]): Monte Carlo methods converge
  at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$ for exactly this reason, which is why they are accurate but slow
